title: identity.oidc_client.created payload
description: The `data` payload of the `identity.oidc_client.created` event: a product registered itself as an OpenID Connect relying party, and the payload is the REGISTRATION'S WHOLE CONTENT. The redirect URIs, the grant types and the scopes are all here because what a registration grants is "this credential may now be delivered to these origins, for these capabilities" — a consumer auditing who holds a credential into a product cannot answer that from the bare fact that a client exists. The registration's own row id is the envelope's `subject` and is NOT repeated in `data`: there is no `oidc_client_id` here, and the two are different values, so conflating them is how a consumer ends up correlating on something it cannot look up. `client_id` below is the string the relying party will present at the token endpoint, not the row. NO SECRET AND NO DIGEST: the raw client secret exists exactly once, in the 201 response to whoever registered it, the row holds a SHA-256 digest, and every event on the platform reaches every subscriber. The envelope is validated by schemas/event-envelope.schema.json; this schema validates what is inside `data`. The file path is the event type with dots as directory separators. See docs/event-naming.md.

client_id.description: The `client_id` string the relying party presents at the token endpoint — 32 random bytes in unpadded base64url, so 43 characters today, with the range being the column's own CHECK rather than core's guess about the entropy. NOT the envelope's `subject`, which is the registration's row id; a consumer that correlates on this string cannot look the registration up by it, and one that correlates on the subject cannot present it. It is a handle that has to be unguessable rather than a cafaye-prefixed id, for the same reason an api key is: a credential you cannot recognise is a credential you cannot revoke in time.

account_id.description: The account the registration belongs to. Present because the subject is the credential and a consumer watching an account's registrations asks the other question — which is the same split `identity.api_key.created` makes and for the same reason.

redirect_uris.description: Where a browser may be sent back to. Deduplicated and sorted by the publisher, so the same set is byte-identical on every registration of it. Never empty, and at most ten. Every entry is checked EXACTLY, never by glob, which is why a wildcard is not a legal value: a registered `https://*.example.com/cb` would be a URI that simply never matches, which reads as a working configuration and is not one. Entries are absolute, `https` — or `http` on the loopback interface only, so a product developing against a local stack still works — and carry no fragment, because the authorization response is appended to the query string and a fragment would end up somewhere the client never reads. `format: uri` is the whole of core's constraint on the shape, and that is narrower than the publisher's: `jsonschema` only checks `uri` when `rfc3987-validator` is installed, core does not install it, and `harness/cafaye_contract.py` DOES decide it — see D22, which is why the guarantee is stated in this sentence rather than left to a validator that may not run.

grant_types.description: Which grants this client may ask for, deduplicated and sorted, and never empty. The vocabulary is closed and it is closed ON PURPOSE rather than pending: `refresh_token` has no store to refresh into, `client_credentials` has no service identity to authenticate as, and `implicit` puts a token in a URL fragment, which is a worse place for a credential than a POST body. A product configured with a grant identity does not implement is refused at registration with a 422 naming the field, which beats a 400 discovered during an outage.

scopes.description: Which claims this client may ask for, deduplicated and sorted, and never empty. `openid` IS ALWAYS AMONG THEM and core does not enforce that here: the registration path refuses a set without it, because a client that cannot ask for it gets tokens with no identity in them, and expressing "contains this one value" needs the `contains` keyword, which `harness/cafaye_contract.py` does not implement — and a keyword the harness cannot decide is a rule it cannot enforce, so using it would have made the schema and the harness disagree about the same document. A consumer that needs the guarantee should treat a payload without `openid` as a publisher bug. Unlike a token request, this path CURATES rather than refuses: unsupported names are dropped, so the column cannot accumulate a promise identity does not keep, and what a product asked for is not necessarily what it got. That is why this is a subset of the four rather than an echo of the request. The OIDC specification's `phone`, `address` and `offline_access` are omissions rather than oversights: identity has no phone column, no address column and no refresh-token store, so advertising any of them would be advertising a claim it cannot fill.

registered_by.description: The user who performed the registration. The `actor`, and the reason the subject is the registration rather than the person: a consumer that has to stop trusting a credential correlates on the credential.
